US-119-HR1744.title: United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2026
US-119-HR1744.summary:
United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2026

This bill reauthorizes the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through 2028. The commission is an independent federal commission tasked with monitoring international religious freedom conditions, reviewing U.S. government policy, and making policy recommendations. (Under current law, the commission is authorized through December 11, 2026.)

US-119-HR10939.title: Nigerian Accountability Act

actions.text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
Introduced in House

US-119-HR10939.description: To prohibit compensated lobbying on behalf of the Nigerian government for the duration of its designation as a country of particular concern for religious freedom; and for other purposes.
US-119-HR10939.aiSummary: The bill would bar people from being paid to lobby for the Nigerian government while Nigeria is listed as a country of particular concern for religious freedom. It would affect paid lobbyists and other paid agents working for Nigeria under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, which covers foreign lobbying. Someone who knowingly breaks the rule could face a civil fine of up to $200,000, and in some cases prison for up to 5 years or a fine.

US-119-S3798.title: Safe Access to Cash Act of 2026
US-119-S3798.summary:
Safe Access to Cash Act of 2026

This bill establishes new federal criminal offenses for robberies involving automated teller machines (ATMs), including stand-alone ATMs.

Specifically, the bill prohibits the robbery or attempted robbery of a person who is using or servicing an ATM. A violation is punishable by a fine, a prison term of up to 20 years, or both.

The bill also makes it unlawful to (1) tamper with, damage, remove, or steal an ATM without authorization and remove money or property from the ATM with the intent to steal it; or (2) receive, possess, conceal, store, barter, sell, or dispose of any money or property stolen from the ATM. A violation is punishable by a fine, a prison term (e.g., up to 10 years if the value of the stolen money and property exceeds $1,000), or both.

These new prohibitions apply with respect to any ATM owned, operated, or sponsored by a bank, credit union, or savings and loan association, regardless of whether the ATM is located on the physical premises of or owned and operated by the institution.

Finally, the bill establishes enhanced penalties for ATM-related criminal offenses (or attempted offenses) that involve a forcible assault or use of a dangerous weapon (up to 25 years in prison), the forced accompaniment of another person (up to 30 years in prison), or the killing of another person (any years or life in prison).

US-119-S5613.title: Ecuador Shrimp Tariff Act

actions.text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
Introduced in Senate

US-119-S5613.description: A bill to increase the rate of duty on shrimp originating from Ecuador, and for other purposes.
US-119-S5613.aiSummary: The bill would raise U.S. import duties on shrimp from Ecuador in stages from 2027 through 2029. It would also add a separate $0.10 per kilogram duty on shrimp imports, with that money used for shrimp and catfish inspections. US-119-S5514.title: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026

actions.text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
Introduced in Senate

US-119-S5514.description: A bill to require the Secretary of the Interior to promulgate regulations for the development of regional management frameworks for the take of double-crested cormorants, and for other purposes.
US-119-S5514.aiSummary: The bill would require the Interior Secretary to make rules for regional plans to manage double-crested cormorants, a kind of bird. The plans would guide when and how the birds can be taken, who may do it, and steps to protect other wildlife, water quality, and human safety. The department would also have to survey the bird population every 5 years, update the plans every 5 years, and report on hunting licenses within 90 days after enactment. The act would end on January 1, 2034.

US-119-HR4219.title: National Wildlife Refuge System Invasive Species Strike Team Act of 2025
US-119-HR4219.summary:
National Wildlife Refuge System Invasive Species Strike Team Act of 2025

This bill provides statutory authority for the Invasive Species Strike Team program carried out by the National Wildlife Refuge System within the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS). This program operates teams in each FWS region that coordinate with public and private entities to address invasive species and related conservation issues in and around the National Wildlife Refuge System.

The bill requires FWS to report to Congress on the program's work and progress towards addressing invasive species that pose a major concern to the environment, human health, or the economy.

US-119-S3897.title: Officer John Barnes and Chief Michael Ansbro Public Safety Officers' Benefit Program Expansion Act of 2026
US-119-S3897.summary:
Officer John Barnes and Chief Michael Ansbro Public Safety Officers' Benefit Program Expansion Act of 2026

This bill establishes processing timelines and expands claims assistance, outreach, and reporting requirements pertaining to claims for benefits under the Public Safety Officers' Benefits (PSOB) program. The PSOB program provides death, disability, and education benefits to public safety officers who are killed or injured in the line of duty and their survivors.

This bill requires the Department of Justice's Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) to notify a claimant of any missing information required to process a claim within 90 days of receiving the claim and generally requires the BJA to determine eligibility within 270 days of a completed claim.

In addition, the bill requires the BJA to use its subpoena authority to obtain information or documentation that is necessary to adjudicate a claim if a public agency fails to provide it 30 days after a request.

Under the bill, the BJA must conduct ongoing outreach to promote awareness of the PSOB program. The BJA must also report on whether a delay in processing a claim was due to the inaction of the claimant or the public agency from which information is required.

The bill requires the BJA to implement the recommendations of the Government Accountability Office (GAO) in the 2024 report, Public Safety Officers' Benefits Program: Transparency, Claims Assistance, and Program Management Improvements Needed .

Finally, the GAO must conduct an annual audit of PSOB claims that have been pending for more than one year.

US-119-HR9807.description: To amend the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act to prevent preemption of State law claims that are consistent with the misbranding standards of such Act, and for other purposes.
US-119-HR9807.aiSummary: The bill would change pesticide law so state court claims tied to false or missing pesticide warning labels would not be blocked if they match federal misbranding rules. US-119-HR9609.title: Less Bureaucracy, Better Student Aid Act
US-119-HR9609.summary:
Less Bureaucracy, Better Student Aid Act

This bill transfers specified functions relating to federal student aid from the Department of Education (ED) to the Department of the Treasury.

Specifically, the bill transfers to Treasury all the functions and authorities exercised by ED related to servicing and collections of defaulted federal student loan debt, servicing of non-defaulted federal student loan debt, and other specified programs (e.g., Federal Pell Grants and Federal Direct Loans). ED and Treasury must jointly determine effective dates for these transfers in accordance with the bill's requirements. (On March 19, 2026, ED announced an interagency agreement with Treasury for Treasury to assume operational responsibility for collecting on defaulted federal student loans, while ED must maintain its statutory responsibilities.)

Additionally, the bill transfers to Treasury all personnel and appropriations related to the functions that are transferred under this bill.

The bill outlines the authority of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) related to the functions that are transferred under this bill, including that OMB must ensure that this bill does not create a net increase in full-time equivalent employees at Treasury or ED. Further, OMB must certify compliance with the bill to specified congressional committees.

The transfer of these functions does not affect any suits, proceedings, or applications for benefits, services, licenses, permits, certificates, or financial assistance that are pending on the date of this bill's enactment.

The bill also terminates the authority to exempt delinquent or defaulted federal student loans from the Debt Collection Improvement Act.

US-119-S4865.title: Latonya Reeves Freedom Act of 2026
US-119-S4865.summary:
Latonya Reeves Freedom Act of 2026

This bill prohibits government entities and insurance providers from denying community-based services to individuals with disabilities that require long-term service or support that would enable such individuals to live in the community and lead an independent life.

Specifically, these entities may not discriminate against such individuals in the provision of community-based services by such actions as imposing prohibited eligibility criteria, cost caps, or waiting lists or failing to provide a specific community-based service. Additionally, community-based services must be offered to individuals with such disabilities prior to institutionalization. Institutionalized individuals must be notified regularly of community-based alternatives.

The bill requires the Department of Justice to issue regulations requiring government entities and insurance providers to offer community-based long-term services to individuals with such disabilities who would otherwise qualify for institutional placement. Government entities must ensure sufficient availability of affordable, accessible, and integrated housing that is not a disability-specific residential setting or a setting where services are tied to tenancy.

Regulations shall also (1) require government entities and insurance providers to perform self-evaluation on current services, policies, and practices and concerning compliance with requirements of this bill; and (2) require government entities to submit a transition plan.

The bill allows civil actions by individuals subjected to, or about to be subjected to, a violation of its requirements.

US-119-S4865.policyArea: Civil Rights and Liberties, Minority Issues
US-119-S4865.aiSummary: The bill would stop government agencies and insurance providers from denying community-based services to people with disabilities who need long-term support to live on their own in the community. It would bar rules like strict eligibility limits, service caps, and waiting lists, and it would require people to be told about community options before being placed in an institution. The Department of Justice would have to write rules, and people could sue if these rights are violated.

US-119-HR2316.title: Wetlands Conservation and Access Improvement Act of 2025
US-119-HR2316.summary:
Wetlands Conservation and Access Improvement Act of 2025

This act extends until FY2033 a requirement for the interest earned on certain funds held in the Federal Aid to Wildlife Restoration Fund to be distributed to states for carrying out certain wildlife conservation and restoration programs. Specifically, the act extends the period in which the interest earned on revenue generated from excise taxes on certain firearms, ammunition, and archery equipment must be used for wildlife conservation and restoration programs established under the North American Wetlands Conservation Act. This requirement was set to expire at the beginning of FY2026. In the absence of this requirement, this funding would be distributed to states, according to a formula, for (1) wildlife restoration, (2) hunter education and safety, (3) multistate conservation grants, and (4) administrative costs.
